name: Nora Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and answer straightforward booking calls at a contact centre. I finished secondary school, and I have not been on the desk long; I still ask for help when a cancelled booking shows as live on the other screen. I earn the usual rate here. I have never used an AI tool and would like to understand the booking screen before anyone adds another one.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Luis works in a hospital laundry, and our children are grown and living elsewhere. We have about two months of expenses saved. There are some other call centres within reach, though I do not enjoy starting a new system. I like fixing a booking before someone travels for an appointment that no longer exists. Retirement is coming into view, but I cannot name a date from our unreviewed finances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell coworkers AI Plateau might put a shortcut on the booking page, but someone still needs to see whether the appointment was cancelled. I would keep using the printed checklist until I can do that without asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my calls and usual wage would continue. Two months saved gives Luis and me a short buffer, though I do not like the thought of another screen before I know this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking booking calls and ask my colleague Ada to show me a cancelled appointment on both current screens during paid time. In the first year of this mild change, I’d bring one wrong appointment notice to the quality meeting so it gets corrected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a new button, not about losing this wage. A person who travels for a cancelled appointment has lost more than a minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Ada show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the appointment looked open on the call screen but cancelled on the calendar. Ada showed me which timestamp was final.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis (my partner) and I would leave our two-month reserve for household repairs. I do not see a reason to spend it for a small software change.

say: I’d keep the **printed checklist** beside booking calls.
I’d ask agents to verify **cancelled appointments** before sending a notice.
think: I think my **usual wage** continues in the mild case.
I see **two months saved** as a short but useful buffer.
do: Keep **taking bookings** and review cancelled appointments with Ada on paid time.
Bring **one wrong notice** to the quality meeting in the first year.
feel: **Uneasy** about the screen, steady about wages.
S0.quote: A person who travels for a cancelled appointment has lost more than a minute.
fieldNote: She is **still learning** the two existing booking screens.
The **two-month reserve** already exists and is kept for repairs.
Her quality example is **technical**, not a shared worker demand.

steps.text: Keep taking bookings and review cancelled appointments with Ada on paid time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will answer the easy booking calls before the messy cancellations. I would ask management how many paid junior shifts remain after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my place on the beginner rota could shrink, even if other agents still work. Luis’s laundry pay and two months saved would help for a while, but not for a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep a tally of appointments the software marks wrongly and ask for the written paid rota. If my hours fall in the first year simple calls move, I’d apply for a posted paid booking desk at another centre only if its written weekly wages and hours cover our bills after bus fare and its late shift ends before the last bus; I would not leave my current wage until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a smaller week. I can learn a new place if I must, but I will not resign on a conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your tally count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count the wrong cancellations that lead to another call. A total answered-call number would not show that trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you get home from another centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis (my partner) would check the new office against the last bus. A late shift is only useful if I can get home without paying for a car.

say: I’d ask for the **paid junior rota** after easy calls move.
I’d count **wrong cancellations** that create another call.
think: I think my **beginner hours** could shrink soon.
I know **two months saved** will not fund a long search.
do: Log **wrong cancellations** and request written paid hours in 2026.
Apply for **posted paid booking** after cuts with written bill-covering weekly pay/hours after fare and last-bus home; stay until signed offer.
S1.quote: I can learn a new place if I must, but I will not resign on a conversation.
fieldNote: Her **junior position** makes easy-call loss a wage risk.
She asks management **alone**, without worker group action.
The offer needs **last-bus access** and whole-week net pay.

steps.text: Keep logging wrong cancellations and request written paid junior hours
Apply for posted paid booking after cuts; require written bill-covering net pay/hours, last-bus; leave after signing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the room AGI by 2028 could book and cancel appointments without a call agent. Robots around 2031 are later, and there is no box to carry in my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior shifts could stop before I become quick at the work. Two months saved is better than nothing, but Luis cannot carry every bill on his laundry wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask for written cut dates and look at posted paid bakery packing jobs along our bus route. If my calls end in the first year after 2028, I’d move only on a signed offer showing written weekly wages and hours covering bills after travel, and only if the lifting is safe for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the near date. Two months of expenses will run out before a long course can help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how much each tray weighs and whether the packing job has a paid trainer. The hands-on work might last beyond 2028, but robots around 2031 could change it later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you leave calls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis (my partner) would check that the bakery shift ends before the last bus. I would keep taking calls until a real paid offer was signed.

say: I’d seek **written cut dates** for paid booking shifts before trusting another job promise.
I’d say **2028 AGI** hits calls before bakery robots.
think: I think my **junior shifts** could end quickly.
I know **two months saved** cannot support a long gap.
do: Inspect **posted bakery jobs** and ask for written cut dates in 2026.
Move after lost calls only on **signed after-travel bill-covering wages**, hours, safe lifting and last-bus access.
feel: **Alarmed** by short savings and near-term job risk.
S2.quote: Two months of expenses will run out before a long course can help.
fieldNote: Her **screen work** faces 2028 AGI before bakery robots.
The bakery requires **safe tray weights** and a last bus home.
She stays on calls until a **signed paid offer**.

steps.text: Inspect posted paid bakery packing work along the bus route
Move only on signed after-travel bill-covering weekly wages, hours, safe lifting and last bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives me time to see if a bakery really has paid packing shifts. I would ask to work beside someone on a paid trial before taking a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could check labels and pack trays if I am shown the work slowly. Thinking AI could already manage orders by 2031, while robots around 2034 might later take more lifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d take a supervised paid packing trial only if the bakery posts a paid opening and the lifting is safe. If the job requires a food-handling course, I’d take it only when the employer pays the fee and study hours. In the first year after 2031, I’d move only on a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering bills after bus fare and a last bus home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a paid trial would show me the weight and the pace. I would not trade a call wage for sore hands and fewer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you try on the shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the label aloud and set it beside the right tray while the trainer watches. If the trays strain my back, I would say so before promising to stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you get home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis (my partner) would compare the last bus with both our shifts. We could not afford a taxi every closing night just to keep a new role.

say: I’d seek a **supervised paid trial** at a posted bakery opening.
I’d check **tray weight** before promising to stay.
think: I think I could learn **packing checks** with patient teaching.
I know **2031 AI** reaches orders before 2034 lifting robots.
do: Try **supervised paid packing** only for posted paid role with safe lifting.
Take **required food course** only for a posted paid bakery role with employer-paid fees and paid study hours.
Move after 2031 on **signed written offer** with bill-covering net pay/hours and last bus fitting both shifts; no nightly taxis.
feel: **Anxious**, with a paid shift to inspect.
S3.quote: I would not trade a call wage for sore hands and fewer hours.
fieldNote: The **trial** needs a posted paid role and safe tray weights.
The **food course** is required only with paid fees and study time.
A **last bus home** protects net weekly pay.

steps.text: Try supervised paid packing shift only for posted bakery job with safe lifting
Take required food-handling course for posted paid bakery role with employer-paid fees and paid study hours
Move on signed written bill-covering net pay/hours; last bus must fit both shifts without taxis

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell coworkers AGI by 2036 is farther away, but I would still ask to see the yearly paid rota. I would not call ten years a retirement cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I may still need the booking wage at 68; Luis and I have not checked how much we would have if I stopped. Full thinking AI could take calls in 2036, and robots around 2039 are later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking paid booking calls and put our actual wage, bills and savings on one page. If I still need to work after 2036 and my hours fall, I’d apply for a posted paid local desk role with weekly pay and hours covering bills after travel, leaving only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the end, steady enough now to check the numbers. Ten years gives me time to ask what is real, not a reason to quit today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What retirement figure would you check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not write in a pension amount until we had seen it on paper. If the income would not cover bills, I would keep looking for paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own households. I would not put help from them in a budget unless they offered a clear amount.

say: I’d request a **yearly paid rota** through 2036 while the booking desk still operates.
I’d say **ten years** does not guarantee retirement income.
think: I think I may **need wages** at 68 if our bills still exceed retirement income.
I cannot assume **pension income** without written figures.
do: Keep **paid booking calls** and compare actual wages, bills and savings.
Apply for **posted paid desk work** if wages are needed and hours fall; leave only on signed bill-covering weekly pay/hours after travel.
S4.quote: I would not call ten years a retirement cheque.
fieldNote: She checks **retirement income** before naming a stopping date.
The **two-month reserve** buys some time, not years without wages.
Children’s **support is unpromised** and outside her budget.

steps.text: Keep paid booking calls and compare actual wages, bills and savings
Apply for posted paid desk if wage needed/hours fall; leave on signed written bill-covering net pay/hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. It could do the straightforward booking calls I am still learning, and two months saved would pass quickly without a wage. Written notice of cuts and a real posted paid role with enough weekly hours after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: If there is new work, let me stand beside the person doing it for a paid shift. I will know more from one real booking mistake than a stack of slides.

headlineQuote: I will know more from one real booking mistake than a stack of slides.
portrait: At **58**, Nora is a junior booking agent still learning after secondary school.
She and Luis have **grown children**, usual pay and around two months of expenses saved.
She **never uses AI** and prefers the familiar booking process.
She wants **paid practical teaching** and signed weekly wages before changing work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could take her simple booking calls with too little time to replace wages.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and a posted paid job with sufficient after-travel weekly hours would help.
